I'm not going to send this. I'm writing it because I've been carrying you around for two years, and my shoulders are tired.

Okay, so, I'm Chaitanya, and the thing nobody tells you about grudges is how boring they get.

My elder brother Anirban sold our grandfather's harmonium. It had been promised to me since I was eight. He didn't ask, he just sold it to a dealer in Siliguri and said, "It was sitting there." For almost three years I brought it up at every family lunch. I kept a mental list.

Then a friend who trains as a counsellor asked me one question over dinner: "What are you waiting for him to say?" I said sorry. She asked, "And if he never does?" I had no answer. I went home and sat on the balcony for a long time.

I decided that night I'd stop dragging it to lunch. Not because Anirban earned it. Because I wanted my Sundays back. He still hasn't apologised. I sleep fine.

Damini had eleven minutes before the last train to Borivali, and Chetan was standing between her and the platform stairs.

"Five minutes," he said. "Please. I've been seeing a counsellor. I know I scared you when I threw the chair. I'm so sorry."

Rain drummed on the station roof. Damini's hand found her phone; her sister Ritu was on speaker, listening, as they had agreed before Damini left the office.

She made herself breathe. "I believe you're sorry, Chetan. And I've forgiven you, honestly, for my own sake. But I'm not meeting you again, and I'm not coming back."

He opened his mouth. She stepped around him, keeping to the lit side of the station. "Ritu, I'm going up now."

On the train she shook for a while. Then she texted her sister: "Did it. On my way." Forgiving him and keeping her distance felt, strangely, like the same decision.

People at my office still call me the Imran who snapped. So let me tell it straight.

Two years ago, in a client review, I tore into Simran, a new analyst on my team. Her numbers had a mistake, and I said, loudly, "Did you even go to college?" She went red, packed her laptop and cried in the stairwell. I heard about it from someone else.

I still wince when I think of that day. But the wince now reminds me, instead of punishing me. That's the difference.

I'm Elizabeth. I live on the ground floor of Irawati's building in Bandra, so I saw the whole cycle business.

A few weeks ago, reversing her scooter in the rain, Irawati knocked over the Fernandes boy's new bicycle and bent the wheel. She rode off. That evening she knocked on my door looking grey and said, "I just left it there, Liz. Who does that?"

The next morning she went up to the Fernandes flat. I heard her through the stairwell: "It was me. I'm sorry. I'll pay for the wheel." She did, that same week.

For days after, she kept bringing it up. "I'm a coward." I finally asked if the boy was still upset. She laughed and said he'd drawn her a thank-you card with a very bent wheel on it.

I'm Sharmila, twenty-five, a pharmacist, which sounds fine, right? But when I was eighteen I wanted to study history. I'd got a seat. My uncle said history was for people who want to be poor, and Baba agreed, and I sat a full year of medical coaching instead. I failed the entrance. Then pharmacy, because it was close.

Tuesday, 11:50 pm

Drafted the resignation again at lunch. Didn't send it. Again.

Tonight the plan was clear as glass: quit Friday, give up the flat, take the train to Goa, figure it out there. Chandrika would understand. Or she wouldn't, and maybe that's also an answer? Six years together and I can't tell if I'm bored with her or bored with everything.

I scared myself writing that.

What is it I actually want? Not Goa exactly. I think I want to feel like my days belong to me. Every day at the agency is someone else's slide deck. Every weekend is errands. I haven't played the guitar since March.

Chandrika asked at dinner why I was so quiet. I said work. Half true.

Tomorrow I'll go to work. I'll send nothing. But I need to find out what's missing before I blow up everything to get it.

Vikas

In Chandpur the government school bell rang at 9:10 every morning, and Nikita had heard it for three years now.

That Thursday, correcting Class 7 copies in the staff room, she found herself looking up night buses to Pune on her phone. Then flats. Then a job she wasn't qualified for.

"You've been on that phone for twenty minutes," said Aditi, the maths teacher, sliding her a cup of chai.

"I'm leaving," Nikita said, and surprised herself. "Maybe next week. I'll just go. My cousin's in Pune."

Aditi raised her eyebrows. "And do what?"

"Anything. I'm twenty-four and I haven't seen anything except this room and that bus stand."

Aditi didn't laugh. She said, "The bus stand I understand. But what do you want to see?"

Nikita opened her mouth and found she didn't have an answer yet, only the itch.

Supervision notes, field office, 14 March. Written by Kalyani, team supervisor.

Ganga came into my room after the village visit and said, "I'm quitting. I'm going to the mountains. I'm done with this." She is twenty-four and one of our steadiest field workers.

My first reaction was alarm; I nearly started listing the reasons she couldn't. I stopped myself. Instead I asked, "What's missing right now?"

She took a while. She said she loves the work but hasn't had a day off in five weeks, hasn't seen her friends, and feels like a machine.

We agreed on two small trials: a proper weekend off starting Friday, and one field day a week with a partner so she isn't alone on the road. We'll check in on the 28th.

Sunday night

Ayesha said it at dinner, between the rajma and the rice: "Ammi, I'm going to leave my job and move to Goa. For good." Her father put his spoon down so hard it rang.

I'll be honest with this page: my first thought was, She's being silly, it's a phase. I almost said it. Then I remembered being twenty-five myself and wanting to run off to Delhi, and how nobody asked me why.

So after the dishes I sat with her on the balcony and asked, "What would Goa give you that you don't have here?"

She said the sea. Then quiet. Then, slower, that she hasn't done one thing for herself in two years. The Goa part is the wrapping.

We agreed she'll book the pottery class she's been talking about since Diwali, and take a long weekend at the coast next month. We'll see what's still true after that.

Hansa
